Who's driving the Dubai Metro?
Nobody. The Dubai Metro is driverless: computers drive every train, and each one keeps a moving bubble of empty track around it.
A control room watches the whole network day and night, and 99.7% of trips run on time.

Send this to someone who still looks for the driver.

Sources: Gulf News, Guinness World Records, Dubai Media Office.
Illustrated explainer, not to scale.

Where does Dubai's tap water come from?
The sea. Plants either boil seawater and catch the steam, or squeeze it through a membrane that stops over 99% of the salt.
Minerals go back in before it reaches your tap.
Dubai can make about 495 million (imperial) gallons a day.

Sources: UAE Government portal u.ae, "Water" ; DEWA, Annual Statistics Booklet 2025 ; Dubai Media Office, DEWA's Jebel Ali complex enters Guinness World Records (2022) ; DEWA, Hassyan Seawater Reverse Osmosis Project ; IEEE TechNav, "Reverse osmosis"

What's holding up Palm Jumeirah?
Sand and rock. No concrete, no steel.
An 11 km rock crescent went in first, then ships sprayed about 94 million cubic metres of sand into place, guided by GPS. Then the sand was vibrated tight so it can't act like a liquid in a quake.

Why pay 55 million dirhams for a number plate?
Because it has one digit. A Dubai plate can have up to five, so a single digit plate is as rare as plates get.
In 2023 plate P 7 sold for AED 55 million at a charity auction in Dubai, a Guinness World Records title. All of it went to a food aid fund.

Send this to the friend who reads every plate in traffic.

Sources: Guinness World Records, Khaleej Times, RTA.
